scientific_disclaimer: Candidate associations represent spatial and temporal proximity associations, NOT definitive proof that satellite observations correspond to the same physical fire front.

primary_region.name: North American Boreal Forest Wildfire Complex

secondary_region.name: Southern African Miombo Savanna Fire Belt
secondary_region.scientific_interpretation_notes: Orbital overpass geometry is the primary governing factor explaining the low match rate (16 candidate associations, 0.73% MODIS, 0.25% VIIRS). Terra overpasses at ~10:30 and Aqua/NOAA-20 at ~13:30 local solar time, creating an inherent ~3-hour diurnal temporal gap. In this region over August 1–2, 2025, MODIS and VIIRS overpass windows had a 2-to-4 hour temporal separation (e.g. MODIS Aqua at 18:00 UTC and VIIRS NOAA-20 at 16:00 UTC on Aug 2), meaning very few observations fell within the 60-minute matching window regardless of physical fire behavior. Rapid savanna fire spread with shorter flaming duration remains a plausible secondary hypothesis, but is secondary to orbital geometry constraints.

limitations_and_sampling_bias: Polar-orbiting satellites provide discrete snapshot overpasses (~10:30 and ~13:30 local time), omitting fire behavior between satellite passes.
Candidate associations reflect spatial-temporal proximity; they do NOT prove identical physical flame fronts without airborne reference lidar or infrared thermal video.

Topological 1:N degree patterns reflect proximity associations consistent with the 7.1x nadir pixel area difference between 1km MODIS and 375m VIIRS, but do not constitute physical proof of sub-pixel flame front splitting.
Scan-angle footprint expansion (bow-tie effect) increases spatial uncertainty near swath edges (up to 4.8 km for MODIS, 800m for VIIRS).
